clinicalPearls: PROP1 deficiency is the single most common identifiable genetic cause of combined pituitary hormone deficiency worldwide and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

The classic hormonal pattern is progressive loss of growth hormone, prolactin, thyroid-stimulating hormone and the gonadotrophins, so affected individuals typically have growth failure and absent or arrested puberty.

Adrenocorticotrophic hormone secretion is usually preserved early but characteristically declines with age, so cortisol deficiency may appear in later childhood or adulthood and demands lifelong monitoring.
Puberty may begin spontaneously and then stall, or fail to start altogether, reflecting the gonadotroph involvement typical of this genotype.
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging may show a normal, small or, distinctively, an enlarged gland; the pituitary can wax and wane in size over time and occasionally mimics a mass lesion.
The posterior pituitary bright spot and the pituitary stalk are typically normal, helping distinguish PROP1 deficiency from stalk-interruption or ectopic posterior pituitary phenotypes.
Extra-pituitary structures are spared, so there are no eye, midline brain or skeletal malformations, unlike HESX1, LHX3 or SOX-related disease.
Recognising the age-dependent evolution, particularly the delayed emergence of adrenal insufficiency, is essential to avoid a preventable adrenal crisis.
reference.pathophysiology: PROP1 (Prophet of Pit-1) encodes a paired-like homeodomain transcription factor expressed transiently in the developing anterior pituitary, where it is required to activate expression of POU1F1 and to specify the Pit-1 lineage (somatotrophs, lactotrophs and thyrotrophs) as well as, indirectly, the gonadotroph lineage. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations therefore impair development of growth-hormone, prolactin, thyroid-stimulating-hormone and gonadotrophin-producing cells, producing the characteristic combined deficiency. PROP1 also normally permits the timely down-regulation of early progenitor factors and the involution of the transitional pituitary; its loss can lead to persistence and expansion of an undifferentiated cell population, which explains the transient pituitary enlargement seen on imaging before the gland later involutes and becomes hypoplastic. The progressive corticotroph failure is thought to reflect a slow, secondary decline rather than a primary developmental block, accounting for cortisol deficiency emerging over years. Because PROP1 acts downstream of the earliest patterning genes and is not expressed outside the pituitary, the phenotype is confined to anterior pituitary hormones without the midline, ocular or skeletal features of more upstream defects. A recurrent small deletion within a repeated sequence of the gene is a common mutational hotspot in many populations.
additionalDifferentials: POU1F1 (PIT-1) deficiency, which spares the gonadotroph axis and preserves puberty
HESX1 mutation with septo-optic dysplasia and midline anomalies
LHX3 deficiency with limited neck rotation and sensorineural hearing loss
LHX4 deficiency with associated hindbrain and skeletal features
Acquired hypopituitarism from a sellar or suprasellar tumour when the pituitary appears enlarged
Idiopathic combined pituitary hormone deficiency without an identified mutation
Isolated growth hormone deficiency before further axes decline
additionalInvestigations: Baseline growth hormone axis with insulin-like growth factor 1, plus prolactin, which is typically low
Thyroid-stimulating hormone with free thyroxine to confirm central hypothyroidism
Gonadotrophins with sex steroids and staging of puberty
Serial assessment of the adrenal axis over time given the risk of late-onset cortisol deficiency
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging, interpreting a normal or enlarged gland in the correct context and repeating if a mass is suspected
Targeted PROP1 sequencing including the recurrent deletion hotspot, or a pituitary gene panel
Bone age radiograph and growth monitoring
redFlags: New adrenal insufficiency emerging years after diagnosis, with risk of crisis during illness
An enlarging pituitary on imaging misread as a neoplasm and inappropriately biopsied or operated
Introduction of thyroxine before confirming adequate cortisol status
Arrest of previously started puberty signalling evolving gonadotrophin failure
Hypoglycaemia or collapse during intercurrent illness in an inadequately cortisol-replaced patient
reference.prognosis: With appropriately sequenced and lifelong hormone replacement, growth and pubertal outcomes are generally good and fertility can often be achieved with gonadotrophin therapy. The main hazard is undertreated or unanticipated adrenal insufficiency, so continued endocrine follow-up is required throughout life.
pitfalls: Mistaking the transient pituitary enlargement for a tumour and pursuing unnecessary surgery
Assuming corticotroph function will remain normal, when adrenal insufficiency characteristically appears later
Starting thyroxine without ensuring glucocorticoid cover and precipitating adrenal crisis
Discharging patients after childhood without arranging lifelong axis surveillance
Attributing stalled puberty to constitutional delay rather than evolving gonadotroph loss
references: Standard textbook of paediatric and adult endocrinology
Clinical guidelines on hypopituitarism and pituitary hormone replacement
Reference text on the genetics of pituitary development
management: Replace growth hormone with recombinant human growth hormone to correct growth failure in childhood
Give levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism, ensuring glucocorticoid status is assessed first to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis
Induce and maintain puberty with sex steroid replacement, and use gonadotrophin therapy when fertility is desired
Monitor the adrenal axis lifelong and introduce glucocorticoid replacement with sick-day dosing and a steroid alert card once ACTH deficiency emerges
Undertake serial pituitary MRI to track the characteristically fluctuating gland size and avoid misinterpreting transient enlargement as a tumour
Coordinate lifelong specialist endocrine follow-up, sequencing hormone replacement appropriately
Provide genetic counselling and screen at-risk relatives, as inheritance is autosomal recessive
